activities.anchor: Shot size is the grammar's nouns
activities.caption: rebuild the size ladder, rung by claim
activities.name: scgSizeOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the size ladder — each rung is a claim about what matters:
items: Extreme wide — the human dwarfed into geography (a figure on a dune ridge)
Wide/long — the environment states itself; bodies act within it
Medium — social distance: waist up, conversation range
Close-up — interiority: micro-expression becomes narrative at face scale
Extreme close-up — a detail becomes the protagonist (a hand, a keyhole, an eye)
config.why: Sizes imply a range: a film that never leaves medium shots feels polite, and one that only erupts into close-ups spends them cheaply — while the insert (the ticking clock, the dripping tap) is the ladder's editorial workhorse.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — the saved close-up
activities.name: scgScarcityPredict

config.q: A director reserves the close-up for one moment in an otherwise medium-shot film. When the close-up finally arrives, the audience reads it as…
choices: A continuity error — the film has jumped rungs on the ladder
An event — scarcity is what gives the size its claim
config.why: Each size makes a claim the audience accepts literally: a film that only erupts into close-ups spends them cheaply, while one that reserves the face scale makes a single close-up land like weather.

activities.caption: pair each angle with its opinion
activities.name: scgAngleMatch

config.prompt: The camera's position is an opinion — pair each height or angle with its claim:

pairs.right: neutral, honest witness — the documentary and humanist default
power, menace, monument — the don shot like architecture

config.why: Ozu's low tatami shots are the exception that proves the rule — a fixed, humble height that dignifies rooms — and POV fuses the audience to a body. Spend opinions on opinion-worthy moments.

activities.anchor: Focal length decides how space itself behaves
activities.caption: drag the divider — one street, two optics
activities.name: scgLensCompare

config.prompt: The same street, two arguments about space — drag the divider between the lenses:

before.label: Wide lens
before.text: Depth exaggerates: near objects loom, backgrounds race away, close faces distort noses outward — and deep focus holds foreground and background sharp enough to argue with each other.

after.label: Long lens
after.text: Space compresses: distances flatten, crowds tighten, the subject isolates in creamy shallow focus — the surveillance aesthetic and the sniper's, one optical fact underneath.

config.why: Between them sits the 50 mm normal — neither comment nor distortion — while the rack focus transfers the audience's eye on command: attention made optical.

activities.anchor: proof the two were never the same move
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the lens briefing
activities.name: scgZoomSpot

config.prompt: One line of this lens briefing is wrong — click it:
lines: A wide lens exaggerates depth: near objects loom, backgrounds race away.
A long lens compresses space, isolating the subject in creamy shallow focus.
Zoom and dolly are interchangeable — both simply bring the subject closer.
Run against each other, they hold the subject's size while the world swells.
That contradiction is the dolly zoom, invented for Vertigo (1958).
config.correction: They move in opposite perceptual directions: a zoom changes magnification while perspective stays frozen; a dolly changes perspective while magnification follows.
config.why: The dolly zoom exists only because the two moves contradict each other — holding the subject's size while the world warps behind it, subjective shock as a spatial contradiction.

activities.anchor: Between shots, conventions do the heavy lifting
activities.caption: cover the two-hander without breaking the map
activities.name: scgAxisBranch

config.root: You are covering a two-hander in a kitchen. The master is set: A screen-left, B screen-right.

start.text: B's single is next. Where does the camera go?

choices.label: Stay on the same side of the line of action
choices.feedback: The 180° rule holds: screen direction stays constant and the audience keeps its mental map.

choices.label: Cross the axis for variety
choices.feedback: Left-right flips — legal only as deliberate disorientation, in battles and panic; in calm conversation it reads as a broken map.

choices.label: Shoot from nearly the same position and size as the master
choices.feedback: Near-identical framings stutter like a missing frame — the jump cut, legal only when Godard-clumsy on purpose.

eyeline.text: Now B glances off screen-left. What carries the audience to what B sees?

choices.label: Cut to what she sees — she looks; what she sees
choices.feedback: The eyeline match stitches the space invisibly.

choices.label: Hold on B and let the dialogue explain
choices.feedback: A fair beat — but the eyeline match is the stitch that makes the fragment read as one room.

coverage.text: Coverage was bought on set — master, mediums, singles and inserts: the edit's power was purchased in the camera department.

config.why: The 180° rule keeps the map, the 30° rule avoids the stutter, and matched eyelines stitch fragments into worlds — a learned dialect, fluent for a century, not a law of nature.

activities.anchor: what is put in the scene
activities.caption: file each choice: camera or design?
activities.name: scgMiseBuckets

config.prompt: Two departments, one frame — file each choice:

items.label: shooting the don from below, like architecture
the period-accurate newspaper on the table
a wardrobe shifting from cool to warm as the character thaws
a rack focus that transfers the audience's eye
blocking that parks a character at frame-edge — 'unstable', wordlessly
a Dutch tilt for the corrupt witness

config.why: The systems cooperate: the camera chooses how to photograph a world the design department has already filled with meaning — Kubrick's corridors and Ozu's tatami flats are arguments about order, artifice and dignity.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — Hollywood's shot tempo
activities.name: scgAslEstimate

config.prompt: On average, how long did a single shot last in 1930s Hollywood?
config.why: About 10–12 seconds — modern blockbusters average 2–4 with action peaks under two, while slow cinema (Tarkovsky, Tsai, Béla Tarr's seven-minute takes) pushes the other way on purpose.
config.context: The tempo tracks technology — lighter cameras, faster editing — and culture: attention economies.
